dimension_1_problem_framing.text: The paper targets data classification problems where quantum machine learning might accelerate data processing by leveraging quantum interference, with a specific focus on making amplitude-based data loading practical despite the exponential gate cost of exact loading and the prior restriction to real-valued vectors. It formulates the task as preparing a parametrized quantum state that approximates a given complex-valued target state for use in a compact-kernel classifier, including an application to credit card fraud detection framed as distinguishing normal from fraudulent transactions. The authors explicitly note that earlier approximate amplitude encoding methods cannot handle complex-valued data, narrowing their applicability to such classification settings.

dimension_2_quantum_method.text: The authors propose an approximate complex amplitude encoding (ACAE) scheme that extends prior approximate amplitude encoding to complex-valued vectors by optimizing a parametrized, hardware-efficient ansatz to prepare a model state that matches the target data state up to a global phase. They replace the earlier maximum mean discrepancy cost with a fidelity-based objective that is sensitive to complex amplitudes and estimate this fidelity and its gradients using classical shadows, while computing gradients via the parameter-shift rule. The method is integrated into a compact amplitude encoding framework and used to implement the compact Hadamard classifier with constant-depth ACAE-based preparation of the training state, and a restricted Ry/CNOT encoder for real-valued test data.

dimension_3_key_results.text: For the Iris experiments, the ACAE training-data encoder reaches a fidelity of 0.994 and the test-data encoders achieve fidelities above 0.999, leading to perfect classification on the easier setosa–versicolor task and some errors on the more challenging versicolor–virginica pair. The authors report that misclassifications in the harder Iris task disappear when exact data (i.e., without approximate encoding) are used, indicating that encoding accuracy affects classification, and they also observe that reducing fidelity from ~0.99 to ~0.7 still keeps accuracy above 80%. In the credit card fraud detection experiments, using four features and small training subsets, all 8 selected test transactions are correctly classified and, in an additional simulation on 48 randomly chosen instances, 42 are correctly classified.

dimension_4_classical_comparison.text: The paper does not present explicit quantitative comparisons with classical classifiers; instead, it notes qualitatively that classical data loading into quantum states would require exponentially many gates and that the CHC can be implemented in a more compact quantum circuit than other quantum classifiers. The effect of encoding errors is indirectly compared against an 'exact data' (non-approximate encoding) quantum baseline in the Iris experiments, where misclassifications are resolved when exact data are used.

dimension_5_stated_limitations.text: The authors acknowledge that prior approximate amplitude encoding could not handle complex-valued data and that MMD-based costs are unsuitable for general complex amplitudes because probabilities depend only on squared magnitudes, motivating their change of objective. They highlight that straightforward fidelity estimation via tomography is exponentially costly in observables, and that classical shadow methods require sampling from n-qubit Clifford unitaries with O(n^2 / log n) entangling gates, which may be challenging to implement in practice. The training procedure entails an O(2^n) classical summation in the fidelity calculation, so runtime scales exponentially with qubit count, and they observe from simulations that the depth of the variational circuit needed to reach high fidelities grows superlinearly with the number of qubits, raising scalability concerns. The authors further note that reaching high fidelity for large systems may suffer from barren plateaus because gradients of global fidelity-based costs can decay exponentially with system size, that 23 qubits would be needed to cover all data in the full fraud dataset, and that the random Clifford measurement required for classical shadows is itself a practical obstacle.

dimension_6_future_work.text: To mitigate training issues such as barren plateaus, the authors point to localized fidelity measurement schemes as a promising direction. They also suggest that improved constructions of Clifford circuits with depth upper bounded by roughly 2n plus logarithmic terms could make the classical-shadow-based fidelity estimation more practical on quantum hardware.

dimension_7_novelty_claim.text: The main claimed contribution is an extension of approximate amplitude encoding to handle complex-valued data via a fidelity-based cost, enabling approximate loading of complex data into shallow circuits, supported by classical-shadow-based fidelity and gradient estimation. Building on this, the paper claims an implementation of the compact Hadamard classifier that avoids the prior critical assumption of exact, exponentially costly state preparation by using ACAE to generate the required quantum state with constant-depth circuits, and demonstrates this approach on both a standard Iris dataset and a credit card fraud detection task.

dimension_8_methodological_notes.text: Methodologically, the authors use a hardware-efficient ansatz and parameter-shift rule for training, with explicit circuit-width reporting (five qubits for the Iris and small fraud instances) and clear specification of training/test splits and tiny training sets (e.g., four samples per class for both Iris and fraud). The Iris experiments involve carefully defined splits and report both fidelities and classification outcomes, including an analysis of misclassifications and their relation to feature overlap and encoding accuracy. For fraud detection, they restrict attention to four PCA-based features (V1–V4), use highly subsampled training data, and then perform both targeted tests and an additional random-instance evaluation; they also carry out a scalability simulation varying qubit counts and depth requirements. All results are obtained on simulators, and no real quantum hardware or noise models are discussed in these codes.

dimension_9_miscellaneous.text: None; all verified codes fit within the primary reporting dimensions.
